strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely question—when can weak, few-step, or domain-mismatched diffusion priors substitute for strong matched priors in inverse problems—that has been observed anecdotally in prior work but not systematically studied.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: multiple tasks (inpainting, Gaussian/nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution), multiple datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN Church/Bedroom, ImageNet), pixel- and latent-diffusion backbones (DDPM, Stable Diffusion 2.1, DiT), comparisons against several strong baselines (DPS, DMPlug, DAPS, DiffPIR, Deep Random Projector), noise-level sensitivity studies, compute-matched comparisons, and even scientific inverse problems from InverseBench.

Combines a clean theoretical narrative (classical posterior-consistency plus a tractable Gaussian-mixture surrogate with proven exponential concentration bounds) with a practical local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic, giving two complementary and testable explanations for the phenomenon.

Honest and systematic study of failure modes (box inpainting, large-factor super-resolution, low measurement-informativeness regimes, high noise), including quantitative degradation curves and qualitative failure visualizations, rather than only reporting favorable cases.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset/checkpoint sources, and algorithmic details (AdamSphere, HoldoutTopK) are provided in the appendix, along with a stated code release.
The proposed AdamSphere optimizer and HoldoutTopK early-stopping rule are simple, well-motivated refinements with ablations isolating their individual contribution (Table 5).
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.2/Proposition A.5) is built on a linear-Gaussian, Gaussian-mixture surrogate model for the prior, which is a substantial simplification relative to the actual few-step DDIM/mismatched diffusion priors and nonlinear forward operators used in experiments; the connection between the formal theory and the realistic diffusion-sampling setting remains largely heuristic and is not rigorously bridged.

The main empirical comparisons contrast a strong-prior baseline solved with a full reverse-diffusion conditioning method (DPS) against weak priors solved with a different algorithm (initial-noise optimization, INO). This conflates the effect of prior strength with the effect of solver choice; the compute-matched comparison in Appendix C.11 shows INO requires 1.5–3x more compute than a single DPS run, which somewhat undercuts the 'weak priors are just as good' framing when compute is accounted for.

The 'identifiable score gap' assumption underlying the main theorem is close to tautological (it essentially requires that the correct candidate has a smaller residual than others) and is validated mainly for random inpainting; its applicability to the tested nonlinear or highly structured forward operators (nonlinear deblurring, super-resolution) is asserted more than rigorously demonstrated.

Reported PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gaps between matched and mismatched/weak priors are sometimes non-trivial (e.g., CelebA inpainting 33.78 vs. 32.62 dB, CelebA super-resolution 31.27 vs. 30.10 dB, and larger gaps in the scientific inverse-problem experiments and DPS-mismatched-prior experiments in Appendix C.9), suggesting the 'nearly as well' claim is sometimes optimistic and depends heavily on task/domain choice.

The local spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic (Section 3.3) shows that short-range pixel correlations are similar across very different domains/sampler strengths, but this could be a fairly generic property of natural images (local smoothness) rather than a mechanism specific to diffusion priors; the causal link between this diagnostic and actual reconstruction success is argued informally rather than established quantitatively.

Statistical robustness of main results (e.g., variance across test images, significance of PSNR differences) is not consistently reported in the main tables, limiting confidence in the magnitude of reported gains versus baselines.

The paper's scope is limited to Gaussian-mixture-amenable, largely linear or mildly nonlinear inverse problems and image domains; results on scientific inverse problems (Appendix C.5) show noticeably larger matched-vs-mismatched gaps than natural images, which the authors acknowledge but which somewhat weakens the generality of the central claim.
